On the other hand, if they miss, the stock may move lower.While the sustainability of the immediate price change and future earnings expectations will mostly depend on management's discussion of business conditions on the earnings call, it's worth handicapping the probability of a positive EPS surprise.Zacks Consensus EstimateThis company is expected to post quarterly earnings of $3.66 per share in its upcoming report, which represents a year-over-year change of +32.6%.Revenues are expected to be $37.03 billion, up 20.6% from the year-ago quarter.Estimate Revisions TrendThe consensus EPS estimate for the quarter has been revised 0.05% higher over the last 30 days to the current level. This is essentially a reflection of how the covering analysts have collectively reassessed their initial estimates over this period.Investors should keep in mind that the direction of estimate revisions by each of the covering analysts may not always get reflected in the aggregate change.Earnings WhisperEstimate revisions ahead of a company's earnings release offer clues to the business conditions for the period whose results are coming out. This insight is at the core of our proprietary surprise prediction model -- the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction).The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a more recent version of the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.Story continuesThus, a positive or negative Earnings ESP reading theoretically indicates the likely deviation of the actual earnings from the consensus estimate. However, the model's predictive power is significant for positive ESP readings only.A positive Earnings ESP is a strong predictor of an earnings beat, particularly when combined with a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), 2 (Buy) or 3 (Hold). Our research shows that stocks with this combination produce a positive surprise nearly 70% of the time, and a solid Zacks Rank actually increases the predictive power of Earnings ESP.Please note that a negative Earnings ESP reading is not indicative of an earnings miss. Our research shows that it is difficult to predict an earnings beat with any degree of confidence for stocks with negative Earnings ESP readings and/or Zacks Rank of 4 (Sell) or 5 (Strong Sell).How Have the Numbers Shaped Up for JPMorgan Chase & Co.For JPMorgan Chase & Co.The Most Accurate Estimate is lower than the Zacks Consensus Estimate, suggesting that analysts have recently become bearish on the company's earnings prospects. This has resulted in an Earnings ESP of -2.19%.On the other hand, the stock currently carries a Zacks Rank of #3.So, this combination makes it difficult to conclusively predict that JPMorgan Chase & Co. Will beat the consensus EPS estimate.Does Earnings Surprise History Hold Any Clue?Analysts often consider to what extent a company has been able to match consensus estimates in the past while calculating their estimates for its future earnings. So, it's worth taking a look at the surprise history for gauging its influence on the upcoming number.For the last reported quarter, it was expected that JPMorgan Chase & Co. Would post earnings of $3.41 per share when it actually produced earnings of $4.10, delivering a surprise of +20.23%.Over the last four quarters, the company has beaten consensus EPS estimates three times.Bottom LineAn earnings beat or miss may not be the sole basis for a stock moving higher or lower. Many stocks end up losing ground despite an earnings beat due to other factors that disappoint investors. Similarly, unforeseen catalysts help a number of stocks gain despite an earnings miss.That said, betting on stocks that are expected to beat earnings expectations does increase the odds of success. This is why it's worth checking a company's Earnings ESP and Zacks Rank ahead of its quarterly release. Make sure to utilize our Earnings ESP Filter to uncover the best stocks to buy or sell before they've reported.JPMorgan Chase & Co. Doesn't appear a compelling earnings-beat candidate. column10: [The June quarter earnings reporting cycle will start grabbing the market’s attention this week, with JPMorgan JPM and the other big banks coming out with their Q2 results.Banks have been going through a tough stretch over the last few months, with the Silicon Valley Bank blowup triggering a speculative frenzy about the next banking victim in the regional banking space. While the immediate pressure has eased and market sentiment on the group has improved, the issue is still very much with us.The big money-center players like JPMorgan have been beneficiaries of the regional bank crisis, as their perceived safety has allowed them to absorb a big part of the deposits fleeing the regionals. We will see this in the Q2 earnings reports from JPMorgan and the others.In addition to JPMorgan, we will see Q2 results from Citigroup C and Wells Fargo WFC before the market’s open on Friday, July 14th.These stocks have lagged behind the broader market, particularly since the early March 2023 onset of the aforementioned regional bank worries, as the chart below shows.Zacks Investment ResearchImage Source: Zacks Investment ResearchWhile these banking leaders are exposed to the same macroeconomic forces, they also have company-specific issues to contend with. Citigroup, in particular, has been going through a seemingly never-ending restructuring, and uncertainty on that front accounts for its underperformance. Wells Fargo appears to have finally put the regulatory issues behind it, but it is far less of a money-center player and more of a jumbo regional operator with a big housing exposure.The expectation is for JPMorgan’s Q2 earnings to be up +23.6% on +20.6% higher revenues. For Citigroup, Q2 earnings are expected to be down -40.7% from the same period last year on +0.2% higher revenues, while the same for Wells Fargo is for +39.9% and +19.1% growth, respectively.The Zacks Major Banks industry, of which all three of these banks are a part, is expected to have +3.8% higher earnings in Q2 relative to the year-earlier period on +11.9% higher revenues. This industry is the largest earnings contributor to the Finance sector, accounting for almost 46% of the sector’s total earnings and nearly double the earnings contribution of the second biggest earnings contributor, which is the Insurance industry.Story continuesFor the Finance sector as a whole, total Q2 earnings are expected to be up +11.1% from the same period last year on +6.3% higher revenues.The table below shows current earnings and revenue growth expectations for the Finance sector’s constituent mezzanine-level industries.Zacks Investment ResearchImage Source: Zacks Investment ResearchIn addition to conventional banking activities, these money-center operators are big investment banking and asset management players with enormous trading operations. The investment banking business has been down for the last few quarters, and Q2 was no different, though more recent activities suggest some ‘green shoots’ on that front. The trading business will also be down relative to last year’s record volumes.All of the profitability gains will be due to the core banking business, with growing loan portfolios and expanded margins helping them enjoy strong net interest income gains. Loan growth is expected to remain positive, though growth is projected to be below the preceding quarter’s pace as demand moderates in response to tighter Fed policies.On the earnings calls, the focus will likely be on trends in loan demand, the health of commercial real estate, credit quality trends, and the health of the overall economy.The Earnings Big PictureRegular readers of our earnings commentary know that we have consistently flagged a favorable turn in the revisions trend since the start of 2023 Q2. This was a shift in the overall revisions trend that had been in place for almost a year prior.Returning to the 2023 Q2 expectations, embedded in the aforementioned earnings and revenue growth projections is the expectation of continued margin pressures, a recurring theme in recent quarters.The chart below shows the year-over-year change in net income margins for the S&P 500 index.Zacks Investment ResearchImage Source: Zacks Investment ResearchAs you can see above, 2023 Q2 will be the 6th consecutive quarter of declining margins for the S&P 500 index.Margins in Q2 are expected to be below the year-earlier level for 11 of the 16 Zacks sectors, with the biggest margin pressure expected to be in the Basic Materials, Construction, Energy, Medical, Conglomerates, Autos, Aerospace, and Tech sectors.On the positive side, the Finance sector is the only one expected to experience significant margin gains, with the Consumer Discretionary sector as a distant second. column4: JPMorgan's Dimon, Staley urge end to shareholders' Jeffrey Epstein lawsuit
column10: [By Jonathan StempelNEW YORK (Reuters) - Jamie Dimon and Jes Staley do not agree on who to blame for JPMorgan Chase's relationship with former client Jeffrey Epstein, but agree that a shareholder lawsuit over their alleged failure to police the disgraced financier should be thrown out.Lawyers for Dimon, the bank's chief executive, and Staley, a former private banking and investment banking chief, urged a dismissal in filings late Thursday in Manhattan federal court.Shareholders led by pension funds in Miami and Pittsburgh have said Dimon, seven other JPMorgan directors and Staley "put their heads in the sand" and ignored internal warnings as Epstein used his accounts to further abuses of young women and girls.Lawyers for Dimon and the directors said there was no showing that either knowingly ignored red flags about Epstein, or that Dimon was involved in keeping Epstein as a client."The claims against Mr. Dimon are based on nothing more than pure speculation and innuendo," the lawyers said.Staley's lawyers, meanwhile, said the shareholders made "no showing whatsoever" that compliance was his job, and that unlike Dimon, "whose writ, as CEO, presumably ran the gamut - Mr. Staley served in discrete roles lower in the corporate hierarchy."The so-called derivative lawsuit seeks to have the defendants or their insurers pay damages to JPMorgan, benefiting shareholders.Lawyers for the two pension funds did not immediately respond on Friday to requests for comment.JPMorgan agreed last month to pay $290 million to settle claims by dozens of Epstein victims.It is also defending against a lawsuit by the U.S. Virgin Islands, where Epstein owned two neighboring private islands.The New York-based bank is suing Staley to cover its losses in both lawsuits, and return eight years of pay.Staley has expressed regret for his friendship with Epstein and denied knowing about his sex trafficking. He also served as Barclays' chief executive from 2015 to 2021.Story continuesEpstein committed suicide at age 66 in August 2019 in a Manhattan jail cell while awaiting trial for sex trafficking.The case is City of Miami General Employees & Sanitation Employees Retirement Trust et al v Dimon et al, U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York, No. 23-03903.(Reporting by Jonathan Stempel in New York; Editing by David Holmes)]

column10: [The market expects JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM) to deliver a year-over-year increase in earnings on higher revenues when it reports results for the quarter ended June 2023. On the other hand, if they miss, the stock may move lower.While the sustainability of the immediate price change and future earnings expectations will mostly depend on management's discussion of business conditions on the earnings call, it's worth handicapping the probability of a positive EPS surprise.Zacks Consensus EstimateThis company is expected to post quarterly earnings of $3.66 per share in its upcoming report, which represents a year-over-year change of +32.6%.Revenues are expected to be $37.03 billion, up 20.6% from the year-ago quarter.Estimate Revisions TrendThe consensus EPS estimate for the quarter has been revised 0.05% higher over the last 30 days to the current level. This is essentially a reflection of how the covering analysts have collectively reassessed their initial estimates over this period.Investors should keep in mind that the direction of estimate revisions by each of the covering analysts may not always get reflected in the aggregate change.Earnings WhisperEstimate revisions ahead of a company's earnings release offer clues to the business conditions for the period whose results are coming out. This insight is at the core of our proprietary surprise prediction model -- the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction).The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a more recent version of the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.Story continuesThus, a positive or negative Earnings ESP reading theoretically indicates the likely deviation of the actual earnings from the consensus estimate. However, the model's predictive power is significant for positive ESP readings only.A positive Earnings ESP is a strong predictor of an earnings beat, particularly when combined with a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), 2 (Buy) or 3 (Hold). Our research shows that stocks with this combination produce a positive surprise nearly 70% of the time, and a solid Zacks Rank actually increases the predictive power of Earnings ESP.Please note that a negative Earnings ESP reading is not indicative of an earnings miss. Our research shows that it is difficult to predict an earnings beat with any degree of confidence for stocks with negative Earnings ESP readings and/or Zacks Rank of 4 (Sell) or 5 (Strong Sell).How Have the Numbers Shaped Up for JPMorgan Chase & Co.For JPMorgan Chase & Co.The Most Accurate Estimate is lower than the Zacks Consensus Estimate, suggesting that analysts have recently become bearish on the company's earnings prospects. This has resulted in an Earnings ESP of -2.19%.On the other hand, the stock currently carries a Zacks Rank of #3.So, this combination makes it difficult to conclusively predict that JPMorgan Chase & Co. Will beat the consensus EPS estimate.Does Earnings Surprise History Hold Any Clue?Analysts often consider to what extent a company has been able to match consensus estimates in the past while calculating their estimates for its future earnings. So, it's worth taking a look at the surprise history for gauging its influence on the upcoming number.For the last reported quarter, it was expected that JPMorgan Chase & Co. Would post earnings of $3.41 per share when it actually produced earnings of $4.10, delivering a surprise of +20.23%.Over the last four quarters, the company has beaten consensus EPS estimates three times.Bottom LineAn earnings beat or miss may not be the sole basis for a stock moving higher or lower. Many stocks end up losing ground despite an earnings beat due to other factors that disappoint investors. Similarly, unforeseen catalysts help a number of stocks gain despite an earnings miss.That said, betting on stocks that are expected to beat earnings expectations does increase the odds of success. This is why it's worth checking a company's Earnings ESP and Zacks Rank ahead of its quarterly release. Small businesses remain optimistic despite economic headwinds
column10: [Small businesses are remaining resilient despite economic challenges, according to the JPMorgan Chase Small Business Macroeconomic Sentiment Tracker for June. Chase Business Banking CEO Ben Walter joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the survey and the state of small businesses.Video Transcript- Majority of small business owners say that their business is exceeding expectations with 71% optimistic about the future despite economic challenges. This according to a recent JP Morgan business banking sentiment survey of small business owners. Well here with a closer look, we want to bring in Ben Walter, CEO of Chase Business Banking. Ben, it's great to see you. So these findings were a little bit surprising given the current macroeconomic environment right now. Small businesses are feeling very optimistic. What's driving that?BEN WALTER: Well, it's interesting. We bank four million small businesses, and we survey 500 of them every month to find out how they're feeling about the economy. And we always see a little bit of a disconnect. So we always see-- if you ask any small business owners, they say my business is doing pretty well. It's doing just fine. And part of that is just being a small business owner. You have to be an optimist.But over the last few months, what we've seen is a wider divergence than we normally see of people saying my business is doing great, but the outlook out there, it's pretty lousy. And that's where people were for the beginning of the year. And a lot of that, you've heard the word vibe session. People not feeling so great. A lot of it having to do with inflation and the stickiness of it.What we've seen over the last few months is that gap has closed. People are now saying actually my business is doing pretty well despite some of the things that people are saying about the economy. And I think it's going to continue to do well. So I think a lot of the things that have been going on in the economy that were sort of new. People hadn't seen inflation for a generation. People hadn't seen labor shortages for who knows how long. Now people are kind of getting used to it. They're adjusting their business models, and they're feeling like they can do well despite those things.Story continues- Yeah. It's interesting to hear how that divergence or at least that divide has closed. And you wonder how much of that is actually a harbinger of what's to come beyond small businesses. What about cost pressures though? How have they been able to navigate that and how has that affected sentiment, especially among small businesses?BEN WALTER: Sure. I mean, at the beginning of the year, it was weighing on them hugely. They certainly still are dealing with it. If you ask small business owners what's going on, 37% of them say you know inflation is still really a problem. But that's still less than half, right? So there's still a majority of them who are saying, I can deal with this. And a majority, you have the number up there. A majority say they are going to raise prices.When you talk to small business owners, and I'm lucky enough to talk to two lots of them every month, when you talk to them, what they say is I'm still probably going to have to raise prices but a lot less than last year, and that's for a couple of reasons. One is they're seeing their prices go up more slowly, and you've seen that in the macroeconomic data. And the other challenge they're having is they're coming up against their customers' ability to pay. And that's particularly true. The closer you are to a consumer business, the more you're running up against that ability to pay. So the more you're starting to constrain, your price increases, and that will eat into margins. But we think there's enough room for that to run.The other numbers you just put up have to do with labor shortages and supply chains. Again, those are things that really spiked during the pandemic. They've come down, but they're still out there. And they're persistent. And that's why I think you're hearing people talk about persistency of some of these challenges. That's why you're hearing people talk about the Fed holding higher for longer. These things are real, and they're not just going away.- Ben, how are they adjusting or really dealing with the labor shortage because it is a massive issue. Are they being forced to offer higher pay, or are they being forced to offer other types of incentives in order to get the workers that they need?BEN WALTER: Yeah. I think there's a few things. So pay has definitely gone up. And we see across the board, they are offering higher pay. In certain segments, I hear lots of pleas to politicians to open up legal immigration. I'm not talking about illegal immigration. I'm talking about legal workers, those numbers are down significantly. Anything in the hospitality industry is really feeling the pinch from that. So they're begging for the doors to be opened back up to get some more workers in the door. That's one of the angles.They've gone to nontraditional sources. How many people have you heard in general about switching careers and finding new things to do? They've gone to nontraditional sources to find new sources of employees and to hire up. And then they're just making do with less. A lot of them are getting smarter, so a lot of the efficiency plays that people have sort of been holding on to for a while, they're now putting them in play. So they're trying to automate with software, they're trying to modernize, and they're trying to figure out how they can squeeze more through with less.- So Ben, that leads me to my question, which is it's great that businesses are feeling good, that sentiment is positive. Have they increased their investments as a result? And if so, where is that going?BEN WALTER: Yeah. They have increased their investments overall, but it's very industry to industry. So if you look across the industry, software investing heavily, professional services investing heavily because they see the returns. Consumer businesses, less so. Hard investment, capital investments, starting to slow down. So it's a real mix in terms of industries and where people see demand.If you look at the industries that are most resilient though, they're going to keep powering through, and we see continued strong investment. And the turmoil in regional banks. Obviously, a massive concern going back to March. How worried are the small business owners that you're talking to about some of the fact that maybe we could see some more pressure when it comes to lending and what that means for their business then going forward?BEN WALTER: I mean, if I try to be a little cynical, our customers we hope are not too concerned about it because they happen to bank with us. But many small business owners do bank with multiple banks and go to multiple places for sources of credit. And we certainly hear pressure about will it be harder for me to get the capital that I need to run my business?So I don't know that you've quite seen the pinch hit the ground yet, but there certainly is concern about that. We are hearing talk about tightened lending conditions across the industry. At JPMorgan Chase, we lend through the cycle. So when things get rosy and everything looks good, we don't tend to lend more. And when things look tighter, we don't tend to really squeeze it down as much either. So we try to lend through the cycle and be there for our customers all the time. A lot of other banks do too. Other banks are feeling a squeeze. And so you'll see a mix of outcomes out there. But access to capital is always an issue for small business owners. And if you do see a real crunch in that, that's going to put the pinch on them.- Ben Walter, great to have you here. CEO of Chase Business Banking. Thanks so much.BEN WALTER: Thank you.]

"That was not evident in the latest jobs report, which included another month of sturdy wage increases. Workers are still in the driver’s seat as labor conditions, while easing, remain historically tight."Story continuesEntering the week, data from the CME Group showed investors pricing in a ~93% chance the Fed raises rates this month and a roughly 40% chance at least two more 0.25% rate hikes are announced by the central bank through November.This week will shape expectations around the Fed's longer term plans, with CPI data expected to show a continued slowdown in inflation pressures. column4: The Q2 Earnings Season Kicks Off
column10: [The June quarter earnings reporting cycle will start grabbing the market’s attention this week, with JPMorgan JPM and the other big banks coming out with their Q2 results.Banks have been going through a tough stretch over the last few months, with the Silicon Valley Bank blowup triggering a speculative frenzy about the next banking victim in the regional banking space. While the immediate pressure has eased and market sentiment on the group has improved, the issue is still very much with us.The big money-center players like JPMorgan have been beneficiaries of the regional bank crisis, as their perceived safety has allowed them to absorb a big part of the deposits fleeing the regionals. We will see this in the Q2 earnings reports from JPMorgan and the others.In addition to JPMorgan, we will see Q2 results from Citigroup C and Wells Fargo WFC before the market’s open on Friday, July 14th.These stocks have lagged behind the broader market, particularly since the early March 2023 onset of the aforementioned regional bank worries, as the chart below shows.Zacks Investment ResearchImage Source: Zacks Investment ResearchWhile these banking leaders are exposed to the same macroeconomic forces, they also have company-specific issues to contend with. Citigroup, in particular, has been going through a seemingly never-ending restructuring, and uncertainty on that front accounts for its underperformance. Wells Fargo appears to have finally put the regulatory issues behind it, but it is far less of a money-center player and more of a jumbo regional operator with a big housing exposure.The expectation is for JPMorgan’s Q2 earnings to be up +23.6% on +20.6% higher revenues. For Citigroup, Q2 earnings are expected to be down -40.7% from the same period last year on +0.2% higher revenues, while the same for Wells Fargo is for +39.9% and +19.1% growth, respectively.The Zacks Major Banks industry, of which all three of these banks are a part, is expected to have +3.8% higher earnings in Q2 relative to the year-earlier period on +11.9% higher revenues. This industry is the largest earnings contributor to the Finance sector, accounting for almost 46% of the sector’s total earnings and nearly double the earnings contribution of the second biggest earnings contributor, which is the Insurance industry.Story continuesFor the Finance sector as a whole, total Q2 earnings are expected to be up +11.1% from the same period last year on +6.3% higher revenues.The table below shows current earnings and revenue growth expectations for the Finance sector’s constituent mezzanine-level industries.Zacks Investment ResearchImage Source: Zacks Investment ResearchIn addition to conventional banking activities, these money-center operators are big investment banking and asset management players with enormous trading operations. The investment banking business has been down for the last few quarters, and Q2 was no different, though more recent activities suggest some ‘green shoots’ on that front. The trading business will also be down relative to last year’s record volumes.All of the profitability gains will be due to the core banking business, with growing loan portfolios and expanded margins helping them enjoy strong net interest income gains. Loan growth is expected to remain positive, though growth is projected to be below the preceding quarter’s pace as demand moderates in response to tighter Fed policies.On the earnings calls, the focus will likely be on trends in loan demand, the health of commercial real estate, credit quality trends, and the health of the overall economy.The Earnings Big PictureRegular readers of our earnings commentary know that we have consistently flagged a favorable turn in the revisions trend since the start of 2023 Q2. Earnings estimates have been stabilizing in the aggregate after consistently coming down for almost a year and have actually started to go up for some key sectors.This combination of favorable macroeconomic developments and optimism about the transformational power of artificial intelligence (AI) appears to be driving market optimism.To get a sense of what is currently expected, take a look at the chart below that shows current earnings and revenue growth expectations for the S&P 500 index for 2023 Q2 and the following three quarters and actual results for the preceding four quarters.Zacks Investment ResearchImage Source: Zacks Investment ResearchThe -9.5% decline in Q2 earnings today is down from -7.2% at the start of the quarter, with estimates for 12 of the 16 Zacks sectors coming down. The biggest cuts to earnings estimates have been for the Energy, Aerospace, and Consumer Discretionary sectors.On the positive side, Q2 earnings estimates increased for the Transportation, Tech, Construction, and Industrial Products sectors.Please note that while 2023 Q2 estimates have come down, the magnitude of negative revisions compares favorably to what we saw in the comparable periods of the preceding couple of quarters. In other words, estimates haven’t fallen as much as they did the last few quarters, not only for Q2 but also for the rest of the year.As noted earlier, we have been pointing out a notable stabilization in the revisions front lately, which roughly coincided with the start of Q2 in April 2023. This was a shift in the overall revisions trend that had been in place for almost a year prior.Returning to the 2023 Q2 expectations, embedded in the aforementioned earnings and revenue growth projections is the expectation of continued margin pressures, a recurring theme in recent quarters.The chart below shows the year-over-year change in net income margins for the S&P 500 index.Zacks Investment ResearchImage Source: Zacks Investment ResearchAs you can see above, 2023 Q2 will be the 6th consecutive quarter of declining margins for the S&P 500 index.Margins in Q2 are expected to be below the year-earlier level for 11 of the 16 Zacks sectors, with the biggest margin pressure expected to be in the Basic Materials, Construction, Energy, Medical, Conglomerates, Autos, Aerospace, and Tech sectors.On the positive side, the Finance sector is the only one expected to experience significant margin gains, with the Consumer Discretionary sector as a distant second. Sectors expected to be essentially flat margins relative to 2022 Q2 are Retail, Utilities, and Industrial Products.The chart below shows the earnings and revenue growth picture on an annual basis.Zacks Investment ResearchImage Source: Zacks Investment ResearchAs noted earlier in the context of discussing the revisions trend of 2023 Q2 estimates, we have been observing a notable stabilization in the revisions trend since the start of April 2023.This stabilization in 2023 earnings estimates represented a notable reversal in the persistently negative trend that had been in place for almost a year. Current expectations for 2023, as represented by the above chart, are down -13.5% since the April 2022 peak.Since the start of 2023 Q2 in April, aggregate earnings estimates for 2023 are essentially flat, with 9 of the 16 Zacks sectors enjoying positive estimate revisions in that time period. Sectors enjoying positive estimate revisions since the start of Q2 include Construction, Industrial Products, Autos, Tech, and Retail.Q2 Earnings ScorecardThe Q2 earnings season will really get going with the July 14th quarterly release from JPMorgan (JPM) and the other big banks. But the Q2 reporting cycle has officially gotten underway already, with results from 18 S&P 500 members out. All of these 18 index members have fiscal quarters ending in May, which we and other data vendors count as part of the June-quarter tally.In fact, by the time JPMorgan comes with its quarterly results, we will have seen such Q2 results from almost two dozen S&P 500 members. Among these 18 index members that have reported already are bellwether operators like Nike, FedEx, Adobe, and others. We have 11 index members on deck to report results, including the aforementioned big banks.Total Q2 earnings for these 18 index members are down -21.5% from the same period last year on +0.6% higher revenues, with 83.3% beating EPS estimates and 66.7% beating revenue estimates.This is too small and unrepresentative of a sample to draw any conclusions from. Still, the comparison charts nevertheless put the Q2 results from these 18 index members with what we had seen from the same group of companies in other recent periods.Zacks Investment ResearchImage Source: Zacks Investment ResearchFor a detailed look at the overall earnings picture, including expectations for the coming periods, please check out our weekly Earnings Trends report >>>> Bank Earnings Looming: What to Expect?  Want the latest recommendations from Zacks Investment Research? column4: JPMorgan's Dimon, Staley urge end to shareholders' Jeffrey Epstein lawsuit
column10: [By Jonathan StempelNEW YORK (Reuters) - Jamie Dimon and Jes Staley do not agree on who to blame for JPMorgan Chase's relationship with former client Jeffrey Epstein, but agree that a shareholder lawsuit over their alleged failure to police the disgraced financier should be thrown out.Lawyers for Dimon, the bank's chief executive, and Staley, a former private banking and investment banking chief, urged a dismissal in filings late Thursday in Manhattan federal court.Shareholders led by pension funds in Miami and Pittsburgh have said Dimon, seven other JPMorgan directors and Staley "put their heads in the sand" and ignored internal warnings as Epstein used his accounts to further abuses of young women and girls.Lawyers for Dimon and the directors said there was no showing that either knowingly ignored red flags about Epstein, or that Dimon was involved in keeping Epstein as a client."The claims against Mr. Dimon are based on nothing more than pure speculation and innuendo," the lawyers said.Staley's lawyers, meanwhile, said the shareholders made "no showing whatsoever" that compliance was his job, and that unlike Dimon, "whose writ, as CEO, presumably ran the gamut - Mr. Staley served in discrete roles lower in the corporate hierarchy."The so-called derivative lawsuit seeks to have the defendants or their insurers pay damages to JPMorgan, benefiting shareholders.Lawyers for the two pension funds did not immediately respond on Friday to requests for comment.JPMorgan agreed last month to pay $290 million to settle claims by dozens of Epstein victims.It is also defending against a lawsuit by the U.S. Virgin Islands, where Epstein owned two neighboring private islands.The New York-based bank is suing Staley to cover its losses in both lawsuits, and return eight years of pay.Staley has expressed regret for his friendship with Epstein and denied knowing about his sex trafficking. He also served as Barclays' chief executive from 2015 to 2021.Story continuesEpstein committed suicide at age 66 in August 2019 in a Manhattan jail cell while awaiting trial for sex trafficking.The case is City of Miami General Employees & Sanitation Employees Retirement Trust et al v Dimon et al, U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York, No. 23-03903.(Reporting by Jonathan Stempel in New York; Editing by David Holmes)]

column4: JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM) Reports Next Week: Wall Street Expects Earnings Growth
column10: [The market expects JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM) to deliver a year-over-year increase in earnings on higher revenues when it reports results for the quarter ended June 2023. This widely-known consensus outlook is important in assessing the company's earnings picture, but a powerful factor that might influence its near-term stock price is how the actual results compare to these estimates.The earnings report, which is expected to be released on July 14, 2023, might help the stock move higher if these key numbers are better than expectations. On the other hand, if they miss, the stock may move lower.While the sustainability of the immediate price change and future earnings expectations will mostly depend on management's discussion of business conditions on the earnings call, it's worth handicapping the probability of a positive EPS surprise.Zacks Consensus EstimateThis company is expected to post quarterly earnings of $3.66 per share in its upcoming report, which represents a year-over-year change of +32.6%.Revenues are expected to be $37.03 billion, up 20.6% from the year-ago quarter.Estimate Revisions TrendThe consensus EPS estimate for the quarter has been revised 0.05% higher over the last 30 days to the current level. This is essentially a reflection of how the covering analysts have collectively reassessed their initial estimates over this period.Investors should keep in mind that the direction of estimate revisions by each of the covering analysts may not always get reflected in the aggregate change.Earnings WhisperEstimate revisions ahead of a company's earnings release offer clues to the business conditions for the period whose results are coming out. This insight is at the core of our proprietary surprise prediction model -- the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction).The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a more recent version of the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.Story continuesThus, a positive or negative Earnings ESP reading theoretically indicates the likely deviation of the actual earnings from the consensus estimate. However, the model's predictive power is significant for positive ESP readings only.A positive Earnings ESP is a strong predictor of an earnings beat, particularly when combined with a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), 2 (Buy) or 3 (Hold). Our research shows that stocks with this combination produce a positive surprise nearly 70% of the time, and a solid Zacks Rank actually increases the predictive power of Earnings ESP.Please note that a negative Earnings ESP reading is not indicative of an earnings miss. Our research shows that it is difficult to predict an earnings beat with any degree of confidence for stocks with negative Earnings ESP readings and/or Zacks Rank of 4 (Sell) or 5 (Strong Sell).How Have the Numbers Shaped Up for JPMorgan Chase & Co.For JPMorgan Chase & Co.The Most Accurate Estimate is lower than the Zacks Consensus Estimate, suggesting that analysts have recently become bearish on the company's earnings prospects. This has resulted in an Earnings ESP of -2.19%.On the other hand, the stock currently carries a Zacks Rank of #3.So, this combination makes it difficult to conclusively predict that JPMorgan Chase & Co. Will beat the consensus EPS estimate.Does Earnings Surprise History Hold Any Clue?Analysts often consider to what extent a company has been able to match consensus estimates in the past while calculating their estimates for its future earnings. So, it's worth taking a look at the surprise history for gauging its influence on the upcoming number.For the last reported quarter, it was expected that JPMorgan Chase & Co. Would post earnings of $3.41 per share when it actually produced earnings of $4.10, delivering a surprise of +20.23%.Over the last four quarters, the company has beaten consensus EPS estimates three times.Bottom LineAn earnings beat or miss may not be the sole basis for a stock moving higher or lower. Many stocks end up losing ground despite an earnings beat due to other factors that disappoint investors. Similarly, unforeseen catalysts help a number of stocks gain despite an earnings miss.That said, betting on stocks that are expected to beat earnings expectations does increase the odds of success. This is why it's worth checking a company's Earnings ESP and Zacks Rank ahead of its quarterly release. Make sure to utilize our Earnings ESP Filter to uncover the best stocks to buy or sell before they've reported.JPMorgan Chase & Co. Doesn't appear a compelling earnings-beat candidate. column4: Big Banks Face Higher Capital Requirements From US Regulators
Bank earnings: Headwinds to watch out for
column10: [Big banks will start reporting their quarterly results on Friday, with JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo on tap. Stephen Biggar, Director of Financial Services Research at Argus Research, tells Yahoo Finance what is he expecting to hear from banks this quarter.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: Tougher capital rules for US banks proposed by the Fed's Barr isn't the only thing that investors are closely watching. Earnings season is just around the corner. And the nation's largest banks are gearing up to report their quarterly results. Here with more on what we can expect, we want to bring in Stephen Biggar, Director of Financial Services Research for Argus Research.Stephen, it's good to see you. So certainly, a challenging set up here for the banks, a higher interest rate environment. We have also the possibility here of stricter regulations. And the implications of that is something that investors are waiting to see. How does this set us up for this round of earnings season?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Yeah, so, well, I think it's going to be, you know, not banks' finest hour in terms of earnings this quarter. Clearly, the higher rate environment that was very helpful in 2022 for net interest margins is having a detrimental effect now. You've got slowing loan growth, just less demand as you have much higher interest rates here. And that's the intended effect of the Federal Reserve.Net interest margins, it looks like they peaked in the fourth quarter of last year. We're likely to see additional pressure sequentially on margins as deposit rates have really increased quite a bit here as banks try to stay competitive with a lot of higher-yielding alternatives out there. And then, of course, on the other bit of lending, the business would be loss provisions.And, you know, we're starting to see some increased delinquencies, particularly in the credit card and auto lending market. So I think banks are going to be conservative here, add to loan loss provisions. And all in all, of course, all three of those will dampen earnings growth a little bit for the quarter.Story continuesAKIKO FUJITA: So you talk about the growth we're likely to see in loan losses, defaults in credit card payments. But we've heard repeatedly about the potential cliff waiting, especially in commercial real estate. What are you going to be looking for, at least in this quarter, in terms of the potential rising risk on that front for banks?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Yeah, definitely, the commercial real estate does, you know, loom as a potential problem area. And we've seen some defaults already kind of pick up there. You know, I think banks did a very good job in the first quarter of laying out the risks there.Typically, for the very large banks, commercial real estate is about 10% of their loan book. Commercial and the office space in particular, which is where a lot of the damage is and the higher delinquency rates, is typically more like, you know, 3% to 4%. It's quite a bit higher, about double that, at the regional bank level, but still, you know, manageable at this point.And of course, the underwriting standards have been better in commercial real estate than they were 5 or 10 or 15 years ago. So that's beneficial for banks. They have generally about a 40-- or 60, I should say, 60% loan to value in there. And, you know, that gives them a fair amount of leeway should these go south.But clearly, a lot of refinancings are coming due in the commercial real estate space over the next three years and definitely among the highest problem areas that we're watching in terms of delinquencies and credit quality.SEANA SMITH: Stephen, we know a lot of the focus in past earnings season most recently have been on guidance. We've already seen a number of the banks, specifically the regionals, already lower their guidance. M&T Bank was one of those names that already lowered their forecast. Do you think we'll see further cuts here over the next several weeks?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Well, I would say, I mean, given that we have earnings coming out at the end of the week, banks have gone into a quiet period. We're probably not going to see additional drop here. A lot of that softer guidance came out during some of the conferences they had at the investment bank. So I think we're, you know, sort of set for the quarter here now that the quarter has ended.But, you know, I think the commentary and the guidance on the earnings calls that we get is probably not going to be a barn burner either, right? We're probably going to, you know, see more of the same banks sort of coming into the last quarter. Actually, some of them were expecting that the Fed would have been done raising interest rates, you know, by mid-year.That looks not to be the case as you look three months later now. Some had expected even a cut by the end of the year. That seems very much off the table now. So I think we're stuck with these higher rates, which will, again, dampen lending growth and slow the economy further, which is bad for credit quality.AKIKO FUJITA: Stephen, it's still a big concern that the regional lenders, the medium-sized banks-- we have seen in the spring, there was, like, JPMorgan swallowing up First Republic. I mean, when you look at the financial space right now, are you expecting more consolidation, you know, not necessarily failed banks, but just seeing where the banks are, especially the medium-sized banks, and the impact they're continuing to take from higher rates?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Yeah, I think-- and, you know, we've seen some support at the regulatory level. There might be some appetite for additional consolidation. I think, you know, most would say it's safe to say we're overbanked in the US. Particularly relative to other countries, we've got about 4,700 FDIC-insured commercial banks in the US today.They all can't make it, I would say, in this environment. I think it, you know, behooves most of them to take a look at partnerships and outright acquisitions if they can't do it themselves. That's tough for a bank, obviously, that wants to maintain its independence, you know, they feel they have the right product set for their local markets, and so forth.But the regulatory aspects here, what happens with the new-- particularly the regulations that are going to be put in place, it's going to make it very hard for banks to compete, for banks to continually elevate. You know, we know that capital cushions only go in one direction, right? And that's up. So they continually have to add more to the capital.Even as they grow larger, you would say it's counterintuitive that the larger banks have to set aside even more. But it doesn't make them safer. It makes them, you know, less prone to failure, certainly, and looks better in the eye of the regulators. So I think we'll see more consolidation here. I don't think we're going to have the number of banks over the next five or 10 years, but I think there's a lot of consolidation that needs to take place.SEANA SMITH: And, Stephen, what is the timeline of that consolidation? Is it something that's going to take years to play out?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Yeah, absolutely. I don't think we're-- you know, banks can only take on so much at a time. The large banks, when they do acquisitions that are sizable, I would say, about 1/3 of their asset base or higher, they tend to take about a year and a half to do that before they even can look at something even more significant. Smaller size or sort of token acquisitions that are in the same service territory, that makes sense. Maybe they can do that a little faster.But yeah, we're talking years here and not just a couple of quarters, obviously. You know, it took about 20 years for banks to have the number of banks that we have in the US. And it's probably going to take another 20, unless we get some, you know, very favorable regulatory environment that actually encourages consolidation. And I don't see that happening.SEANA SMITH: So, Stephen, given all this, given the very challenging sort of backdrop that we're in right now, who is best positioned in this environment?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Well, it'll still favor of the large banks, the JPMorgans, Bank of Americas, even Morgan Stanley, and some of the super regionals, I would say, like the Truist Financial, PNC Financial, U.S. Bancorp. These are banks that have already largely met the-- or can more easily meet the higher capital requirements. It will take them a matter of quarters, let's say, to no more than two years to reach these higher capital levels that are most likely to be in place.And we do expect, of course, the banks to sail through this year's stress test. The CICA results came in, but those are going to get more stringent going forward. We're going to have a scenario where interest rates spike over the forecast period versus decline, which has been the way it's worked with stress tests in the past.The Basel III international regulations are going to get more strict and severe as well. They're going to add a couple of more nuances to scenarios and what happens with banks, in particular about risk weighted assets and trading assets as well. So that will affect the Morgan Stanley's and Goldman Sachs of the world in particular. So I think those are still well positioned.Banks in the kind of $100 billion to $250 billion range or even $50 on their way to $100 billion are really going to have, you know, a tougher time. So I'd stick with the larger banks. They've got great earnings potential here. They're well diversified. They've got good yields at this point.And of course, many of these have suffered in the decline. They're well underperforming the market at this point. And that'll create some opportunities for investors.SEANA SMITH: All right, well, we'll start seeing these quarterly results later on this week. Stephen Biggar of Argus Research, thank you so much.STEPHEN BIGGAR: Thank you.]

column4: UPDATE 1-Morgan Stanley hires JPMorgan's North America M&A head -sources
column10: [(Adds more details and background in paragraph 2, 4 and 7)By Svea Herbst-Bayliss and Anirban SenJuly 10 (Reuters) - Morgan Stanley has hired senior investment banker Marco Caggiano from JPMorgan Chase & Co , where he led the bank's North America mergers and acquisitions (M&A) business, people familiar with the matter said on Monday.Caggiano, a veteran investment banker who spent 23 years with JPMorgan, will join Morgan Stanley as vice chairman of M&A, the sources said. JPMorgan has not yet named a replacement for Caggiano, the sources said.The sources requested anonymity because the matter is confidential. JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley declined to comment.Morgan Stanley's global M&A franchise is currently led by John Collins, who previously served as global head of healthcare investment banking at the bank. In the Americas, Morgan Stanley's M&A franchise is led by veteran dealmakers Tom Miles and Brian Healy.At JPMorgan, Caggiano had worked on several high-profile situations, including advising Twitter Inc on its $44 billion sale to Elon Musk, Take Two on its $12.7 billion acquisition of mobile video game maker Zynga, and toy maker Hasbro Inc on its board fight with hedge fund Alta Fox.Caggiano trained as a lawyer and worked at Paul Hastings before he joined JPMorgan. He was co-head of North America M&A before Chris Roop, the other co-head, exited JPMorgan last year to join Jefferies Financial Group Inc.Several top bankers have recently left firms such as Goldman Sachs, Bank of America and Barclays to either join direct competitors or smaller peers, amid a global slowdown in dealmaking that has forced top Wall Street banks to trim their investment banking groups and accelerate other cost-cutting moves. (Reporting by Svea Herbst-Bayliss in Rhode Island and Anirban Sen in New York; Editing by Greg Roumeliotis and Andrea Ricci)]

column4: Banks are fighting to keep deposits. How much is it costing them?
column10: [Bank deposit rates are the highest in a decade and a half. That’s good news for savers, but bad news for lenders as they prepare to release their second-quarter results.US banks spent the last several months competing with each other to keep or bring back depositors following the turmoil that took down three sizable regional institutions and triggered outflows across the banking system.That scramble pushed rates on savings accounts to 5.05% at the end of the second quarter, according to Bankrate, their steepest level since February 2008.Read more: The best high-yield savings account rates for July 2023The challenge for banks across the US is that these higher funding costs are eating into a key measure of profitability known as net interest margin, which measures the difference between what lenders make from their loans and what they pay for their deposits.That will likely act as a drag on results for some banks in the quarter, especially the mid-sized regional institutions that ran into trouble last spring, while reducing estimates of what they can earn for the rest of the year.“The surprises this quarter will be for the banks that do not lower expectations,” Wells Fargo bank analyst Mike Mayo told Yahoo Finance.Banks, added Argus Research's Stephen Biggar, "have a deposit conundrum."'Green shoots'?These pressures will be at the front of mind for investors starting Friday as they digest the first set of second quarter earnings from JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Citigroup (C), Wells Fargo (WFC), and State Street (STT).Bank of America (BAC) and Morgan Stanley (MS) report next Tuesday and Goldman Sachs (GS) next Wednesday. A slew of other regional banks will also report in the coming weeks.Some of the biggest US banks are expected to once again demonstrate their resilience and diversity, showing they can continue to charge more for their loans while leaning on their sprawling franchises to generate additional revenue.Story continuesJPMorgan, Wells Fargo, and Bank of America are all expected to show jumps in net income when compared to the year-earlier period, according to analyst estimates, while Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley are expected to report profit declines.JPMorgan's headquarters in New York City. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig, File) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)Those that are more dependent on investment banking, such as Goldman, are expected to be particularly challenged by a recent drought in deal making.Global investment banking revenues for the second quarter fell by 8% from the first quarter and 52% from a year ago, according to Dealogic. However, the business improved through the second half of the quarter, prompting some observers to predict “green shoots” ahead.“I’m turning to believing investment banking will not have great earnings but they’re going to be surprising, and I think better than expected,” said Dick Bove, a bank analyst with Odeon Capital.Investors will also be watching to see whether many of these big banks increase the amounts they set aside for future loan losses, a sign that they expect the US economy and credit conditions to worsen.“We're starting to see some increased delinquencies, particularly in the credit card and auto lending market,” said Biggar, Argus Research's director of financial services.'A huge amount of problems'Smaller regional banks are clearly not under the same amount of pressure as they were in March, when the fall of Silicon Valley Bank triggered panic across the country.But they still “face a huge amount of problems,” Bove said.The core issue is an aggressive campaign by the Federal Reserve to bring down inflation with higher interest rates. That campaign is lowering the value of the assets banks hold, such as bonds, while deposit costs creep higher and loan demand slows.Read more: Why now is a good time to open a savings account“We view accelerating deposit costs, not accelerating deposit outflows, as the most significant headwind to earnings for the next several quarters,“ Manan Gosalia, a regional bank analyst for Morgan Stanley, said in a research note.Higher rates have traditionally worked to the advantage of banks since it allows them to charge more for their loans than their deposits.But the panic of the spring “has changed the calculus a bit” for some banks, the Fed’s vice chair of supervision Michael Barr said Monday. Some lenders “are now paying up more for deposits,” and the Fed is “paying careful attention to that.”Silicon Valley Bank was seized on March 10. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu, File) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)The Fed has made it clear that more hikes are coming this year. Regulators are also preparing new capital requirements for banks with more than $100 billion in assets that will force some to hold greater buffers against losses. That will increase the stability of those lenders but will also make it even more difficult to earn robust profits in the near term.Many banks have already warned at a conference in June that their net interest margins are going to drop by more than they expected for the quarter or the year, including executives for US Bancorp (USB), Citizens Financial Group (CFG), Comerica (CMA), Huntington (HBAN), KeyCorp (KEY), and Zions (ZION).“I’ve only been a banker for 10 years, so I haven’t seen a time when we’ve needed deposits as an industry as much as we do now,” Darrin Williams, the CEO of the 58-branch Southern Bancorp, told Yahoo Finance.The amount Southern Bancorp is paying customers has risen 600% since the Fed’s interest rate hiking cycle began, Williams added.“Our cost of funds continues to rise just because our customers demand that.”The larger banks aren’t immune to some of these same challenges.“Deposits will continue the trend of being slightly down from here,” Jennifer Piepszak, co-CEO of JPMorgan Chase's massive consumer and community bank, said at a conference in June.The bank has predicted it will earn net interest income of $84 billion in 2023, but if the deposit pressure keeps up, that figure could experience a “mild reprice,” she said.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]
